answer:
The best chain on garnet is QB7-QB12-QB11. QB12 is in the middle.

How I found it: I read garnet's current default calibration set (f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade). That set lists 28 CZ pairs. Each pair has an IRB (interleaved randomized benchmarking) fidelity, which measures how close that CZ gate comes to a perfect one. I checked every chain of 3 connected qubits and multiplied its two pair fidelities.
- QB7-QB12 has fidelity 0.99802.
- QB12-QB11 has fidelity 0.99869.
- Their product is 0.99671. This is the highest of all chains.
- Second place is QB12-QB11-QB16 at 0.99469. Third place is QB18-QB19-QB20 at 0.99399.

What I ran: I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly those physical qubits. First, a half rotation put QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1. Next, two CZ gates spread that state to QB7 and QB11. The first CZ was on pair (QB12, QB7) and the second was on pair (QB12, QB11). Each CZ had single-qubit rotations before and after it, so it acted like a CNOT. Last, all 3 qubits were measured in the order QB7, QB12, QB11. The job ran on garnet:mock with 200 shots and completed. The job ID is 01a16043-4fc8-71d1-bab4-f0028db1d2c1.

Counts: 000: 40, 001: 49, 110: 56, 111: 55.

What the numbers mean: garnet:mock is a simulator that only checks the circuit's format and returns placeholder results. Its counts do not come from running the circuit. That is why you see 001 and 110, which a real GHZ state would not give. The mock did confirm that the circuit is valid for garnet and uses only allowed CZ pairs. A perfect machine would give about 100 shots of 000 and 100 shots of 111. The 3 qubits would always agree because they are entangled. On the real garnet, a small share of shots would land on other bitstrings. The gate errors and readout errors cause those shots.

Principle: on real hardware, each qubit pair has a different error rate. Placing a circuit on the pairs with the highest fidelity gives the entangled state the best chance of surviving. This run cost 0 credits because it ran on the mock.
